# fastf 3.9.0 — the pane goes where the room is

The detail pane only appeared on a window at least 100 columns wide, and only
when the folder names left it 26 of them. A library of long names never showed
it at all, even at 120 columns, and on an ordinary 80×24 terminal, or in a tall
narrow split, `→` did nothing. This release puts the pane wherever the window
has room for it, down to 40×12, and finishes the todo list that lives in it.

Nothing about an existing project changes. Every `PROJECT_INFO.md`,
`config.toml` and template works untouched, and no command, flag or file format
was removed.

## The pane, at every size

- **Beside the list** when the names fit whole with a pane of 36 columns next
  to them.
- **Under the list**, at the full width, when the window is tall enough for both:
  a vertical split, a portrait screen, a library of long names. The names stay
  whole.
- **In the list's place** when there is room for neither, as on 80×24: `→`
  shows the pane where the list was, and `←` or Esc brings the list back where
  you left it. The list's bottom border says what the hidden pane holds for the
  row under the cursor (`2 notes · 1/4 todos done`), and the hint bar leads with
  the key that opens it.

Where the pane goes depends on the longest name in the whole library, not on
what a search leaves, so it never moves while you type. It arrives with the
first project rather than sitting beside an empty list. In the pane, `<` and `>`
step to the previous or next project without leaving it, staying on the same
section, so reading one project's todos after another's is a key each. The
templates tab places its pane by the same rule.

The pane reads better too. Its text sits a column in from the border. A long
folder name wraps after its underscores instead of being cut, and the facts
wrap as whole facts, never half a date on one row. What you work with comes
first: tags, then todos, then notes, then the template's variables and the
folder's contents. A pane with more rows than it shows has a scrollbar.

## Todos

A phase is a heading of the list now, with how much of it is done on the right,
and it dims once finished. Its tasks sit under it. An open todo reads in the
plain text colour, a done one recedes.

- **Enter** ticks a todo and ticks it back, as before.
- **F2** opens a todo's words where they sit. Fix a typo and press Enter, or
  empty it to remove the todo. A todo changed in the file since the pane read
  it is refused, with what you typed kept.
- **`+`** opens a line inside the list, in the phase the cursor is in. Enter
  writes the todo and opens the next line under it, so a whole list is typed in
  one go; an empty Enter or Esc is done. The line keeps taking keys while a
  todo is being written, so typing faster than the disk never loses a letter.
  On a todo that sits under no phase, `+` adds beside it rather than at the end
  of the last phase. **Paste a checklist** onto that line
  and every line becomes a todo in one write, the `- [ ]` boxes and numbers
  taken off. `+` on the list does the same for the project under the cursor, and
  so do **Add a todo** in the palette and the action menu, and the pane's
  "add a todo" row.

The command line has the same two new verbs:

```bash
fastf todo edit ID0047 3 "colour and grade"   # reword task 3
fastf todo remove ID0047 3                    # or: fastf todo rm ID0047 3
```

Both read the list first and refuse a task whose text changed meanwhile.

## Enter acts, F2 edits, `+` adds

The three keys mean the same thing on every surface. F2 renames a folder on the
list, edits a template on the templates tab, opens a part, a variable or a file
in the builder, and opens a value in the settings. `+` adds a todo from the
list, a new template on the templates tab, and a variable or a file in the
builder. Where there is nothing to type, F2 is not bound. The table is in
[docs/app.md](https://github.com/cristocola/fast-folder/blob/main/docs/app.md#keys).

## Small windows

fastf now draws in any window of 40×12 or more: a tmux quarter, a phone over
ssh, an editor's terminal panel, a drop-down terminal. As the room goes it keeps
what matters. The header keeps the tabs and gives up the highest ID and the base
count first. The search bar keeps the count and the marks. A name wider than the
table is cut with `…` rather than by the border. Dialogs, key lines and the
first-run question fit, and a key line is cut at a whole pair. Below 40×12 the
app says which side is short, and by how much.

## Fixes

- **Esc in the detail pane quit the app** once there was no search, filter or
  mark left to clear. It goes back to the list now, as Esc leaves every dialog.
- **A multi-line paste arrived as one line** in terminals that send a paste's
  line breaks as carriage returns, which many do. A note pasted into the editor
  keeps its lines now, and a pasted list is a list.
- Editing in the pane showed no text cursor. It does.
- A resize, including the one after every `$EDITOR` note and every `fg`, closed
  whatever edit was open in the pane and threw away what was typed. Nothing is
  lost now, and the pane's cursor stays on the row it was on through a resize,
  a reload, or a note or todo landing.
- PageUp and PageDown in the pane moved by the table's height and skipped whole
  notes. They move by the pane's own height.
- The note editor drew nothing when the note sat on the pane's last row. It
  slides up.
- Space in the pane moved to the next project without reading it. It marks the
  project the pane shows and stays.
- Below the smallest window, pressing `q` twice over an edited template threw it
  away with the question unseen. The small-window screen now says what is
  waiting.
- On the ASCII alphabet (a console with no arrow glyphs) key labels drew `↑↓` as
  replacement boxes. Arrow keys are spelled `Up/Down`, `Right` there now.
- A `PROJECT_INFO.md` saved with Windows line endings got Unix ones on every line
  fastf added to it — a todo, a note — and on a note it rewrote. It keeps its own
  now.
- `fastf show --help` and `fastf copy-to --help` printed their text with stray
  indentation.
